threads.body: [General] This fallback can expose malformed user-info as `server.address`. For example, `jdbc:mariadb:failover://user:123,a?x=y@h1:3306,h2:3306/db` makes the candidate authority `user:123,a`; both pieces pass `hasValidHostPorts`, and this early return then publishes the username/password fragment as the configured target. This contradicts the fail-closed credential handling immediately above. Before accepting the candidate, detect that the text after the last `@` is itself an endpoint (or endpoint list) and return `null`; alternatively, parse this ambiguity with driver-specific URL grammar rather than treating any syntactically valid pre-`?` list as hosts.

replies.body:
Addressed in ebb440118040d25bf2e32d2bea9b3d69dbdffe53.

Analysis: The query fallback validated only the text before `?` and returned a multi-host candidate before it inspected the text after `@`. It now extracts the endpoint-shaped prefix after `@` and rejects the fallback when that prefix is a valid host or host list.

Upsides: Malformed credentials cannot become `server.address`, and the existing handling for `@` inside query values remains intact.

Downsides: The fallback rejects ambiguous malformed URLs instead of reporting a configured target.

threads.body: [General] The opaque-target detection only recognizes the exact substring `(address=`. Valid descriptor formatting such as `(ADDRESS = ...)` or `( ADDRESS=...)` therefore falls through into the legacy parsed-host map; a mapping for an Oracle descriptor with two such blocks will also match the unrelated host `oracle`. Use the same whitespace-tolerant address-token recognition as the JDBC parser before deciding to add the parsed-host fallback.

replies.body:
Addressed in 71973fbc65e49844f59e143c2555204dcab0a4f0.

Analysis: The exact substring check misses valid Oracle address tokens with spaces around the name or equals sign. A case-insensitive pattern now recognizes the same token forms as the JDBC parser. The resolver skips the parsed-host fallback when it finds two address blocks.

Upsides: Spaced Oracle descriptors match only their full configured target. They no longer create an unrelated mapping for the driver name.

Downsides: Mapping setup now runs a small regular expression scan instead of two substring searches.

[General] This brackets every IPv6 host even when no port is emitted. Consequently an all-default-port list such as `jdbc:postgresql://[2001:db8::1],[2001:db8::2]/db` becomes `[2001:db8::1],[2001:db8::2]`, contrary to the linked issue's requirement that IPv6 literals are bracketed only when paired with ports. Keep the existing URL-rendering behavior if needed, but render configured-target brackets conditionally on a non-null emitted port.

This issue also appears on line 430 of the same file.

replies.body:
Addressed in 51c1de33b2f049a8f250b3813b8a487197ff54b4.

Analysis: Configured targets used the URL host formatter. That formatter brackets IPv6 literals even when it omits their ports. A configured-target formatter now adds brackets only when it also emits a port. URL rendering keeps its existing behavior.

Upsides: Default-port IPv6 target lists no longer contain unpaired brackets. Mixed and non-default port lists remain unambiguous.

Downsides: Configured-target formatting now uses a separate small helper from URL formatting.

threads.body: [General] A valid single-host MariaDB URL such as `jdbc:mariadb:failover://h1?sessionVariables=email='user@example.com',sql_mode=ANSI` makes both authority helpers return `null`, so this branch clears the parsed/default host and port and returns before the normal URL parsing. The same query shape is supported for multi-host URLs by the new tests, but for a singleton it now drops `server.address` and `server.port` in both stable and legacy modes. Please preserve ordinary parsing for this singleton case while retaining the fail-closed path for genuinely ambiguous multi-target credentials; `hasMultipleTargets()` currently misclassifies this input too, so both decisions need to be corrected together.

replies.body:
Addressed in 83973f3af650876452aa7025647805516391fb55.

Analysis: The shared query check treated a comma after `@` as evidence of a second target even when the text before `?` was one valid endpoint. It now recognizes that single endpoint before classifying the `@`. This fixes both authority extraction and multi-target detection. Prefixes with multiple entries still use the strict ambiguity checks.

Upsides: Plain and address-block MariaDB singleton URLs keep their host and default port when a query value contains `@` and a comma. Malformed multi-target credentials still fail closed.

Downsides: The query check now sanitizes the authority once to confirm that it contains one valid endpoint.

threads.body: [General] This still allows malformed user-info to become `server.address` when the text after `@` is a single `address=(...)` target. For example, `jdbc:mariadb:failover://user:123,a?x=y@address=(host=h1)/db` makes `suffixAuthority` fail `isEndpointAuthority`, so the fallback returns and publishes `user:123,a`. Recognize a single sanitized address entry as an endpoint too, so ambiguous credentials continue to fail closed.

replies.body:
Addressed in 14486f4b278a2e73392e5838fa97861d245fa234.

Analysis: The endpoint predicate recognized plain singleton targets and multi-entry address blocks, but not one address block. Reusing the single-endpoint sanitizer lets the suffix check identify that target and reject the malformed user-info.

Upsides: A single MariaDB address block after malformed credentials cannot expose the credential prefix as `server.address`. Valid singleton address-block queries remain supported.

Downsides: Endpoint checks now run the single-entry sanitizer before trying the multi-entry sanitizer.

threads.body: [General] The address-block sanitizer accepts `=` inside the extracted host, so `address=(host=password=secret)(port=3306),address=(host=db2)(port=3306)` publishes `password=secret,db2` as `server.address`. This can expose credential-shaped values even though the linked semantic-conventions proposal requires `server.address` to contain no sensitive information. Reject invalid address-host values before constructing the sanitized entry.

replies.body:
Addressed in 2e2ec0aeff65d7a7bf8c1da1bdb9d380a8e0d4cd.

Analysis: Both cases bypassed the same host-entry validation. Address-block hosts now use that validation before sanitization. A single port separator now requires text before the colon, so a port-only entry is invalid.

Upsides: Credential-shaped address values and port-only entries cannot become configured targets. Valid host names, bracketed addresses, and IPv6 literals keep their existing behavior.

Downsides: Address-block host values now follow the same restrictions as plain host entries.

threads.body: [General] A port-only list entry is accepted as a valid endpoint because a colon at index 0 reaches `parsePort`. For example, `jdbc:postgresql://h1,:5433/db` produces the invalid configured target `h1,:5433` instead of failing closed, contrary to the complete-list validation described by this PR. Require a non-empty host before the single port separator.

threads.body: [General] This accepts every value with multiple colons as valid, even when it is not an IPv6 literal. For example, `jdbc:postgresql://not:an:address,h2/db` passes sanitization; `extractHostPort` then treats the first colon as a port separator and truncates that entry to `not`, so stable telemetry reports `server.address=not,h2` instead of failing closed. Require this branch to validate the complete value as an IPv6 address (including the supported zone syntax) before accepting the list.

replies.body:
Addressed in e468c42fc35107d62330f02d07ea17d9d8e87ee2.

Analysis: The multi-colon branch accepted arbitrary text before extraction. Reusing `DbServerTargetBuilder.isValidHost` validates the complete unbracketed value as an IPv6 literal and preserves the validator's supported zone identifier syntax.

Upsides: Malformed multi-colon targets now fail closed, while valid scoped IPv6 literals remain available for configured server telemetry.

Downsides: Multi-colon host text that is not a valid IPv6 literal is no longer reported.

threads.body: [General] A present but malformed address-block port is silently treated as if no port was configured. For example, `address=(host=h1)(port=secret),address=(host=h2)(port=3306)` drops the first `port` token and can normalize to `h1,h2` instead of rejecting the malformed target list. Detect a reserved `port` property that does not parse exactly (and duplicate port properties) and return `null` so this path preserves the PR's fail-closed behavior.

replies.body:
Addressed in d8a1b0a2a667b1a6bbe94b475c272e69069a0812.

Analysis: Address-block sanitization only recognized numeric `port` properties, so malformed reserved properties disappeared before parsing. Explicit ports were also checked only for integer syntax. The sanitizer now recognizes every reserved `port` property, rejects malformed or duplicate values, and applies the database target port range before any target path renders the list.

Upsides: All configured target paths fail closed for malformed, duplicate, zero, or out-of-range ports. Valid explicit ports retain the existing normalized output.

Downsides: Previously accepted out-of-range ports and malformed address-block `port` properties no longer produce configured target telemetry.

threads.body: [General] The special-target path validates hosts but never validates explicit port ranges. For example, an unknown-driver URL such as `jdbc:unknown://h1:70000,h2:70000/db` takes this branch because `defaultPort` is null and emits `h1:70000,h2:70000`, whereas the normal `DbServerTargetBuilder` path rejects ports outside 1–65535. Apply the same range validation before rendering special targets so malformed lists fail closed consistently.

threads.body: [General] This endpoint test again misses Oracle descriptors whose `ADDRESS` blocks are adjacent rather than comma-separated. A declarative peer such as `oracle:thin:@(description=(address = ...)(address = ...))` is indexed exactly, but also falls through to the parsed host map as host `oracle` with no port or path, so an unrelated `server.address=oracle` resolves to this service. Treat multi-address descriptors (including spaced/case variants) as exact-only before adding the host fallback.

replies.body:
Addressed in e7798b9351730ef693cc7f5dc2d6edbc3f0d2a4d.

Analysis: The resolver only treated top-level commas as evidence of multiple endpoints, so adjacent Oracle ADDRESS groups reached the parsed-host index even though the peer had no single host identity.

Upsides: Adjacent Oracle descriptors now stay in the exact-address index, and tests cover lowercase and spaced uppercase ADDRESS spellings.

Downsides: The resolver performs one case-insensitive pattern scan when a peer authority has no top-level comma.

threads.body: [General] Duplicate `host` properties are silently collapsed to the first value. For example, `address=(host=h1)(host=h2),address=(host=h3)` is accepted and reported as `h1,h3`, even though the driver-facing entry is ambiguous and may select `h2`. Reject a second host token, as is already done for duplicate ports, so malformed groups fail closed.

Analysis: The address sanitizer checked only the first host match, so it accepted an ambiguous address block while already rejecting the same shape for ports.

Upsides: Malformed address blocks now fail closed instead of reporting a host that may differ from the driver's target.
